oneSentence: A method that turns words in an image or scanned page into machine-readable text that software can search, copy and analyse.
plainExplanation:
Optical character recognition, or OCR, takes an image that contains writing and converts the visible letters and numbers into digital text. The input might be a scanned paper form, a photo of a street sign, or a PDF that is really just page images.

A typical OCR system first looks for where text appears in the image. It may straighten the page, improve contrast, and separate lines or words from the background. Then it predicts which characters are present. A character is a single letter, number, or symbol.

The output is text data, often with information about where each word was found on the page. That means people can search the document, copy a sentence, translate it, or send the text into other software such as summarisation or named entity recognition.

OCR is often confused with reading meaning. OCR mainly converts shapes of letters into text. Understanding what the text means is usually a later step handled by language tools. OCR quality also depends heavily on image quality, handwriting style, font, script, and whether the language is well supported.

everydayAnalogy.title: A clerk retyping notices from photos
everydayAnalogy.story: A city office receives phone photos of printed notices from different buildings. A clerk looks at each photo, finds the text area, mentally straightens the tilted image, and retypes the words into a searchable spreadsheet. Later, the team can sort the messages by words like “urgent” or “meeting”. The clerk is not judging whether the notice is true or important yet, only converting what is visible into editable text.

mapping.aiElement: images or scans used as OCR input

mapping.analogyElement: the clerk finds the text area

mapping.aiElement: preprocessing such as deskewing and contrast adjustment
converting character shapes into machine-readable text

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A human clerk can use broad world knowledge, guess missing letters from context, and handle unusual layouts with little explanation. OCR systems do not work like a person retyping. They rely on trained pattern-matching and image-processing methods, and they can fail badly on blur, handwriting, mixed scripts, or rare fonts even when the general topic seems obvious to a human.

visual.title: How OCR turns a page image into searchable text
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to describe OCR as a multi-step process from image input to text output, and explain that recognising letters is different from understanding meaning.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. It starts with a photographed or scanned page, then shows text regions being found, then character recognition, then machine-readable text ready for search or later language tasks. Read from left to right.

steps.label: 1. Image input
steps.explanation: A page arrives as a scan, photo, or image-only PDF. At this stage, the computer has pixels, not editable text.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a document thumbnail with a folded corner and faint text lines. Add a small label: scan/photo/PDF image.

steps.label: 2. Prepare and locate text
steps.explanation: The system may straighten the page, improve contrast, and mark where lines or words appear.
steps.visualInstruction: Show the same page slightly straightened with highlighted rectangles over text lines. Include a small tilt-correction icon.

steps.label: 3. Recognise characters
steps.explanation: Inside those text regions, the system predicts letters, numbers, and symbols based on their shapes.
steps.visualInstruction: Zoom into one highlighted word and show image letters transforming into typed characters, with a few confidence dots above them.

steps.label: 4. Output usable text
steps.explanation: The result becomes searchable, copyable text, sometimes with position data so each word can be linked back to its place on the page.
steps.visualInstruction: Show plain text in a search box and a cursor selecting words, plus a small overlay linking text back to page locations.

visual.interaction: Hovering over each stage reveals one example: a tilted receipt image, detected text boxes, recognised word, and final searchable text. Keyboard focus moves through the same stages in order.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram explains OCR in four connected stages. First, a document exists only as an image made of pixels, such as a scan or photo. Second, the system prepares the image and marks where text appears, for example by straightening the page and finding text lines. Third, it recognises characters within those marked regions and converts their shapes into letters, numbers, and symbols. Fourth, it outputs machine-readable text that can be searched, copied, or passed to later language tools. The key point is that OCR changes visible writing into text data; understanding the meaning is a separate task.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-panel flow replaces animation. Each panel shows one stage with arrows between them: image input, text location and cleanup, character recognition, and searchable text output.

workedExample.scenario: A team photographs a printed meeting notice on a wall to capture the details quickly.
workedExample.input: Photo text: “Health clinic closed on 14 May. Reopens 16 May at 08:30.”
process: The OCR system receives the phone photo and detects one main text block on the notice.
It corrects the slight tilt and increases contrast so the letters stand out from the paper background.
It recognises the characters line by line and outputs digital text with word positions.
A simple keyword rule then flags the message as time-sensitive because it contains a closure date and reopening time.
workedExample.result: Searchable text: “Health clinic closed on 14 May. Reopens 16 May at 08:30.” The text can now be copied into a message log or sorted with other notices.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN office wants to build an internal search tool over a large collection of scanned guidance documents and image-only PDF manuals.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: OCR can turn those page images into searchable text so staff can find the right section by keywords instead of opening files one by one.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Use only approved internal systems and review the output, especially if documents contain sensitive operational, personal, protection-related, or security-sensitive information; do not upload such files to a public AI service.

whyItMatters:
Many important documents are trapped inside images: scans, photos, old PDFs, forms, signs, and archives. Without OCR, a computer cannot easily search or reuse that writing. With OCR, organisations can find information faster, reduce manual retyping, improve accessibility, and feed text into translation, search, or analysis tools.

For non-specialists, the key decision point is reliability. OCR can save time, but mistakes matter when dates, names, case numbers, medicine labels, or legal wording are involved. You may need human checking, especially for poor-quality scans, handwriting, uncommon scripts, or low-resource languages. Knowing what OCR can and cannot do helps you choose the right workflow and the right level of review.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: OCR understands the meaning of a document.
commonMisconceptions.correction: OCR usually focuses on turning visible characters into text. Understanding topic, sentiment, entities, or instructions is a separate language task that may happen afterwards. A system can copy the words correctly and still not interpret them well.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If text looks clear to a person, OCR will always get it right.
commonMisconceptions.correction: People use context and background knowledge to fill gaps. OCR depends on image quality, script support, layout, font, blur, shadows, and training data. It may confuse similar shapes such as 0 and O or miss text in a complex table.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: OCR only works on printed paper documents.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Printed scans are common, but OCR is also used on photos, screenshots, signs, labels, and image-only PDFs. Handwriting can sometimes be processed too, but that is often harder and less accurate than clean printed text.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: OCR changes a picture of writing into text that software can search and copy.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: OCR is a pipeline that converts text-bearing images into structured text output. It often includes image preprocessing, text detection or segmentation, line and word grouping, and character or sequence recognition. Older systems relied more on hand-engineered image features and character templates. Many modern systems use machine learning to detect text regions and predict character sequences directly from image patches or text lines. The output may include recognised text, confidence scores, and coordinates for each line or word. OCR should be distinguished from speech-to-text, which converts audio rather than images, and from later natural language processing steps that interpret the extracted text.

keyTakeaway: OCR does not read meaning first; it turns visible writing in images into usable text so people and software can work with it.

quickCheck.question: What does OCR mainly produce from a scanned page?
options: A summary of the document's main ideas
Machine-readable text copied from the visible writing
A spoken audio version of the page
A judgement about whether the document is important
quickCheck.explanation: OCR's main job is to convert written characters in an image into digital text. Summarising, reading aloud, or judging importance are different tasks that may use the OCR output later.
